constitutive_assumptions: Quasi-static equilibrium is assumed for motion transitions and force/moment balances.
Motor torque is evenly distributed between the two symmetrical drive shaft sprockets (tau_m / 2 = tau_rc2).
Parasitic friction forces (Delta f) and torques (Delta tau) on contact surfaces outside the thread are assumed to be negligibly small.
Pitch radii of the drive shaft sprocket and motor sprocket are identical; pitch radii of sprocket 1 and sprocket 2 are identical.
Friction follows Coulomb friction behavior with constant static (mu_st) and kinetic (mu_kn) friction coefficients.
No slippage occurs between the conveyor belt and the grasped object during pull-in mode.
control_variables: Motor rotational velocity (held constant at 14 deg/s during mechanism characterization tests).
Initial separation distance between the fingertip and target object (set to 10 mm in mechanism A tests).
Calculated motor torque cutoff limit (0.8 Nm in mechanism A tests).
Motor rotation angle limit (180 deg in mechanism B tests).
Target motor torque thresholds (tau_target_m = 0.3 Nm for standard objects; 0.1 Nm for fragile egg) corresponding to desired contact forces (28 N and 9 N).
dependent_variables: Fingertip rotational angle (theta_f) and sprocket rotational angles (theta_sp1, theta_sp2).
Torque transmitted through roller chain 2 (tau_rc2) and calculated motor torque (tau_m).
Linear pull-in displacement of the grasped object (d_PI).
Mode switching sequence behavior and stability.
Object grasp and release success across varied test scenarios.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The robotic gripper realizes three sequential functional modes (grasping, finger-bending, and pull-in) driven by a single motor through two self-motion switching mechanisms that respond to motion obstruction.

SMS mechanism A utilizes a screw feed mechanism to switch between finger-bending/pull-in rotation and grasping translation depending on whether chain resistance torque exceeds lead-screw frictional resistance.
SMS mechanism B employs a preloaded screw and a mechanical hard-stop to switch from finger-bending rotation to belt-conveyor translation once bending reaches 90 degrees.

A thread lead angle of lambda = 30 degrees provides stable sequential motion switching, whereas lambda = 20 degrees results in erratic mixed motion and lambda = 60 degrees significantly reduces achievable tip force.
The gripper can perform in-hand reorientation and translation to retrieve objects from tight, boxed shelf compartments where standard parallel grippers cannot operate.
The single-motor gripper achieves a maximum payload of 30.8 N in grasping mode and 29.4 N in pull-in mode with an initial finger width of 40 mm.

experimental_setup: SMS mechanism A single-finger evaluation testbed: fingertip unit locked to sprocket 2 to isolate grasping/bending; instrumented with an IMADA ZTS-500N force sensor for tip force, an IMADA HTGS-10N torque sensor for chain torque, and two Logicool C1000eR cameras tracking optical markers for finger translation and rotation; evaluated at thread lead angles of 20, 30, and 60 degrees.

SMS mechanism B single-finger evaluation testbed: finger body fixed and grasping mode omitted; instrumented with an IMADA HTGS-10N torque sensor between motor and sprocket 1, and a front-facing Logicool C1000eR camera tracking markers on the fingertip frame and sprocket 2; evaluated at screw tightening torques of 0.0, 0.46, and 0.75 Nm.

Confined-space grasping test setup: gripper mounted on a robotic manipulator operated via manual teaching to retrieve objects under four constrained geometries (open-top box in shelf with internal obstacle boxes, rotation-restricted box, partially covered box, and off-axis orientation requiring in-hand re-grasping).
Tabletop grasping test setup: grasping and releasing varied objects (15 mm die, 1.0 kg bottle, fragile egg, spherical golf ball, deformable toy doll) and releasing via motor reversal.
future_work: Evaluating the effectiveness of the gripper in other manipulation scenarios.
Developing an optimization method for gripper design parameters.
Integrating sensory feedback to achieve fully automated object pickup.
independent_variables: Thread lead angle (lambda = 20 deg, 30 deg, 60 deg) in SMS mechanism A.
Tightening torque of the preloading screw (T_scw = 0.0, 0.46, 0.75 Nm) in SMS mechanism B.
Motor rotational direction (forward vs. reverse) and motor angle/displacement.
Target object physical properties (mass, size, shape, stiffness/fragility).
Confined space geometry and obstacle configurations (Cases 1 through 4).
limitations_inferred: Reliance on mechanical friction thresholds and preloading may make motion-switching repeatability susceptible to wear, thermal changes, or surface contamination over time.
Indirect force estimation via motor current and lead-screw kinetics assumes known, constant friction coefficients that may fluctuate in real-world environments.
Symmetrical dual-finger operation relies on balanced external contact; asymmetric object contact or external disturbances could lead to uneven finger behavior.
Sequential mode triggering depends on unidirectional motor rotation and mechanical stops, preventing direct, arbitrary mode jumping without reversing or altering mechanical states.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Incorporating SMS mechanism B increased finger thickness compared to simple thin-finger grippers, creating a disadvantage for insertion into extremely narrow gaps.
Downsizing components to thin the fingers introduces a trade-off with finger stiffness and structural durability.
The robotic arm equipped with the gripper required manual teaching for manipulation tests; autonomous operation requires additional sensors.
A trade-off exists between fingertip motion speed and achievable tip force governed by the lead angle lambda.
Tightening torque T_scw must remain within a bounded range so that the motor torque required for mode switching does not exceed motor capacity.
main_results: Successfully demonstrated sequential activation of finger-bending, grasping, and pull-in modes using unidirectional rotation of a single motor via two passive self-motion switching mechanisms.

Identified lambda = 30 deg as the optimal thread lead angle for stable motion switching, confirming theoretical predictions of unstable motion at lambda = 20 deg and reduced tip force at lambda = 60 deg.
Demonstrated that screw preload torque T_scw = 0.46 Nm avoids premature pull-in activation while keeping motor torque requirements within operating limits.
Successfully executed in-hand translation (40-50 mm) and rotation to extract objects from four confined-space shelf configurations where parallel-jaw grippers fail.
Demonstrated stable grasping of diverse objects (15 mm die, 1.0 kg bottle, raw egg, golf ball, toy doll) and controlled release via motor reversal.
Achieved experimental payloads of 30.8 N in grasping mode and 29.4 N in pull-in mode.
modeling_methods: Quasi-static force and moment equilibrium modeling of lead-screw drive and chain-sprocket transmission.
Classical lead screw mechanics relating thrust force and actuation torque through thread lead angle and friction coefficient.
Static and kinetic friction threshold conditions governing transition between nut translation (grasping) and nut rotation (bending/pull-in).
Kinematic transmission modeling relating roller radius, gear train reduction, and motor rotation to object pull-in displacement.
performance_metrics: Maximum payload in grasping mode: 30.8 N
Maximum payload in pull-in mode: 29.4 N
Finger width in initial extended configuration: 40 mm
Target grasping force range: 9 N (fragile egg) to 28 N (general objects)
Pull-in translational distance: 40 mm to 50 mm demonstrated
possible_gap_implications: Presents a mechanical strategy to execute multi-modal in-hand manipulation with a single actuator, reducing weight and complexity for end-effectors in space-constrained robotic manipulation.

Highlights the viability of passive self-motion switching mechanisms in replacing multi-actuator systems, though sensitivity to friction, component wear, and lack of autonomous perception remain challenges for industrial deployment.
paper.research_objective: To develop, analyze, control, and validate a compact robotic gripper driven by a single motor with thin fingers that achieves sequential grasping, finger-bending, and pull-in modes via novel self-motion switching mechanisms for in-hand manipulation in confined spaces without environmental support.
paper.research_problem: Retrieving objects from confined spaces (such as boxes on shelves) requires changing object position and posture to prevent collisions, which typically requires a large manipulator workspace. Existing in-hand manipulation end-effectors either require multiple actuators (increasing size and complexity) or rely on environmental supports/external forces (applicable only in restricted situations).
paper.title: Single-Motor Robotic Gripper With Three Functional Modes for Grasping in Confined Spaces
